entries.title: Governor
entries.plain: Runs California's state government. Signs or vetoes the bills the Legislature passes, writes the state budget proposal each year, appoints judges, and directs the state's response to emergencies.

source.name: California Secretary of State, Official Voter Information Guide (June 2010, archived)

quotes: As the state's chief executive officer, oversees most state departments and agencies and appoints judges. Proposes new laws and approves or vetoes legislation. Prepares and submits the annual state budget. Mobilizes and directs state resources during emergencies.
ask: What would they put first in the state budget, and what would they cut?
Which kinds of bills would they sign, and which would they veto?
How would they choose judges and the people who run state agencies?

entries.title: Lieutenant Governor
entries.plain: Takes over if the governor can't serve, and presides over the State Senate, where they can cast a tie-breaking vote.

source.name: California Secretary of State, Official Voter Information Guide (June 2010, archived)

quotes: Assumes the office and duties of Governor in the case of impeachment, death, resignation, removal from office, or absence from the state. Serves as president of the State Senate and has a tie-breaking vote.
ask: Are they ready to step in as governor?
How would they use a tie-breaking vote in the State Senate?

entries.title: Secretary of State
entries.plain: Runs statewide elections, makes campaign and lobbying money public, and registers businesses and trademarks.

source.name: California Secretary of State, Official Voter Information Guide (June 2010, archived)

quotes: As the state's chief elections officer, oversees statewide elections and provides public access to campaign and lobbying financial information. Supports California business by registering and authenticating certain types of businesses and trademarks
ask: How would they run elections that are both secure and easy to vote in?
How would they make campaign and lobbying money easier to follow?

entries.title: Controller
entries.plain: The state's accountant. Keeps the books for all public money, runs the state payroll, handles unclaimed property, and audits state operations.

source.name: California Secretary of State, Official Voter Information Guide (June 2010, archived)

quotes: As the state's chief fiscal officer, serves as the state's accountant and bookkeeper of all public funds. Administers the state payroll system and unclaimed property laws.
Conducts audits and reviews of state operations.
ask: What would they audit first, and why?
What experience do they have with accounting, auditing or managing large budgets?

entries.title: Treasurer
entries.plain: The state's banker. Invests state money and sells the state's bonds (how California borrows).

source.name: California Secretary of State, Official Voter Information Guide (June 2010, archived)

quotes: As the state's banker, manages the state's investments. Administers the sale of state bonds and notes, and is the investment officer for most state funds.
ask: How would they balance safety and returns when investing state money?
What experience do they have with investing or public finance?

entries.title: Attorney General
entries.plain: The state's top lawyer. Runs the Department of Justice, represents California in court, and oversees law enforcement, including district attorneys and sheriffs.

source.name: California Secretary of State, Official Voter Information Guide (June 2010, archived)

quotes: As the state's chief law officer, ensures that the laws of the state are uniformly and adequately enforced. Heads the Department of Justice, which is responsible for providing state legal services and support for local law enforcement. Acts as the chief legal counsel in state litigation. Oversees law enforcement agencies, including county district attorneys and sheriffs.
ask: Which kinds of cases would they make a priority?
When would they take someone to court on the state's behalf?
How would they oversee local law enforcement?

entries.title: Insurance Commissioner
entries.plain: Regulates the insurance companies that sell in California: licenses and examines them, enforces insurance laws and writes the rules under them, and answers people's complaints about insurers. Runs the state Department of Insurance.

source.name: California Secretary of State, Official Voter Information Guide (June 2010, archived)

quotes: Oversees and directs all functions of the Department of Insurance. Licenses, regulates, and examines insurance companies. Answers public questions and complaints regarding the insurance industry. Enforces California insurance laws and adopts regulations to implement the laws.
ask: How strictly would they regulate insurance companies, and what would that mean for prices and coverage?
What would they do for people with complaints about their insurer?
What experience do they have with insurance or consumer protection?

entries.title: Superintendent of Public Instruction
entries.plain: California's top public-schools official. Runs the state Department of Education, carries out the State Board of Education's policies, and gives direction to local school districts.

source.name: California Secretary of State, Official Voter Information Guide (June 2010, archived)

quotes: As the state's chief public schools official, provides education policy and direction to local school districts. Directs all functions of the Department of Education and executes policies set by the State Board of Education.
ask: What would they change about how the state supports local schools?
What experience do they have in education?

entries.title: Board of Equalization
entries.plain: An elected state board that oversees California's property tax system, keeping it consistent from county to county, plus the state taxes on alcohol and on insurance companies.

source.name: California State Board of Equalization, About BOE

quotes: Today, the BOE is constitutionally and statutorily responsible for overseeing California's property tax system, as well as the Alcoholic Beverage Tax and Tax on Insurers.
Each of the BOE's constitutional and statutory duties is critical to promoting a consistent and uniform property tax system throughout the state.
ask: How would they keep property taxes assessed the same way in every county?
What experience do they have with taxes or property assessment?

entries.title: King County Prosecuting Attorney
entries.plain: Leads the county's prosecutors, who bring charges for every felony in King County and for misdemeanors outside city limits. Also the county government's lawyer in civil cases.

source.name: King County Prosecuting Attorney's Office

quotes: The Prosecuting Attorney's Office represents the state and county in both criminal and civil legal matters.
We are responsible for prosecuting all felonies in King County and all misdemeanors in unincorporated areas of King County.
We are also the County's law firm.
ask: Which crimes would they make a priority?
When would they seek jail, and when other options?
What experience do they have as a prosecutor or in court?

entries.title: CU Regent
entries.plain: A member of the elected board that runs the University of Colorado. The board supervises the university and controls its money.

source.name: University of Colorado Board of Regents

quotes: The board is charged constitutionally with the general supervision of the university and the exclusive control and direction of all funds of and appropriations to the university, unless otherwise provided by law.
ask: How would they handle tuition and what students pay?
What would they want the university to spend more, or less, on?

entries.title: Larimer County Assessor
entries.plain: Sets the value of every property in the county (homes, businesses, farmland) for property taxes. If you disagree with your value, you can protest it with the Assessor in May.

source.name: Larimer County Assessor

quotes: The County Assessor is responsible for valuing all real and personal property, including mobile homes, residential and commercial properties and agricultural land for property tax purposes.
The Assessor determines the equitable value of property to ensure that each taxpayer pays only their fair share of the taxes.
Anyone who disagrees with changes in the actual value of real property can object or file a protest with the Assessor in May .
ask: How would they keep property values accurate and easy to understand?
How would they handle protests from property owners?

entries.title: Larimer County Treasurer
entries.plain: Collects the county's property taxes. Doesn't decide how much tax you owe; ask the Assessor about your property's value.

source.name: Larimer County Treasurer & Public Trustee

quotes: The Treasurer does NOT determine the amount of tax to be collected.
For more information on the value of your property or the amount of the taxes collected, please contact the Larimer County Assessor's Office .
ask: How would they make paying property taxes easier?
What experience do they have managing public money?

entries.title: Larimer County Surveyor
entries.plain: A professional land surveyor who represents the county in property-line (boundary) disputes and, when the county commissioners ask, surveys county land such as road rights-of-way.

source.name: Larimer County Surveyor

quotes: The Larimer County Surveyor is a professional land surveyor and is responsible for representing the county in boundary disputes.
When authorized by the Board of County Commissioners, the Surveyor conducts surveys of county property including rights-of-way.
ask: What surveying experience and credentials do they have?

entries.title: Larimer County Coroner
entries.plain: Investigates sudden or unexpected deaths in the county, including traffic deaths, homicides and suicides, and determines the cause and manner of each death.

source.name: Larimer County Coroner

quotes: The Office of the Larimer County Coroner/Medical Examiner is responsible for investigating all sudden and/or unexpected deaths throughout the county.
Through an investigation, a determination is made as to the cause and manner of death.
This includes death while a person is in custody or within 24 hours of being admitted to a hospital, as well as all fatal traffic deaths, homicides, and suicides.
ask: What medical or death-investigation training do they have?
How would they work with families and with law enforcement?

entries.title: U.S. Representative
entries.plain: Your member of the U.S. House of Representatives: one of up to 435 who write and pass federal laws, elected every two years to represent your congressional district.

source.name: U.S. House of Representatives, The House Explained

quotes: House of Representatives makes and passes federal laws.
The number of voting representatives in the House is fixed by law at no more than 435, proportionally representing the population of the 50 states.
Also referred to as a congressman or congresswoman, each representative is elected to a two-year term serving the people of a specific congressional district.
ask: Which federal laws would they work to pass, or to block?
How would they serve people in this district?

entries.title: Superior Court judge
entries.plain: A trial judge on the county's Superior Court, where most California cases start: criminal and civil cases, plus family, probate, juvenile and traffic cases. The judge (sometimes with a jury) hears the evidence and decides by applying the law.

source.name: Judicial Branch of California, California Judicial System

quotes: Most cases in California start in one of the 58 superior courts, or trial courts, handling both civil and criminal cases, such as family, probate, mental health, juvenile, and traffic cases.

facts.plain: In a trial, a judge (and sometimes a jury) hears testimony and evidence and decides the case by applying the law to the facts.

source.name: Judicial Branch of California, Superior Courts

quotes: In trial (superior) courts, a judge and sometimes a jury hears witnesses' testimony and other evidence and decides cases by applying the relevant law to the relevant facts.

entries.title: Water Replenishment District director
entries.plain: A director of the water district that manages the groundwater basins under southern Los Angeles County, which supply about four million people in 43 cities. Voters created it in 1959 to stop over-pumping. Its board sets the district's replenishment charge.

source.name: Water Replenishment District of Southern California, Annual Comprehensive Financial Report 2022

quotes: The WRD is a special water District that was established in 1959 by popular vote to counteract the effects of over pumping of groundwater from two major groundwater basins in Los Angeles County.

WRD manages the Central and West Coast groundwater basin (collectively, the "Basins") which provide groundwater for approximately four million residents in 43 cities of southern Los Angeles County (County).
WRD Board of Directors voted to increase the Fiscal Year 2022 Replenishment Assessment to $394.00 per acre-foot.
ask: How would they keep groundwater clean and plentiful?
How would they decide the district's charges?

entries.title: Monterey Park City Clerk
entries.plain: A part-time elected official who runs the City Clerk's office. The office is where candidates file campaign finance statements and officials file conflict-of-interest statements.

source.name: City of Monterey Park, City Clerk's Office

quotes: As a part time elected official, the City Clerk is responsible for establishing policies, guidelines and procedures for the operation of the City Clerk's office.
The City Clerk serves as the filing officer for candidate campaign finance statements and conflict of interest statements by elected, appointed officials and key city employees.
ask: How would they make campaign and conflict-of-interest filings easy for the public to see?
What experience do they have running an office?

entries.title: King County Council
entries.plain: One of nine councilmembers who make King County's laws and policies and adopt its budget. Each represents a district of over 260,000 people, elected without party labels for four years.

source.name: Metropolitan King County Council

quotes: As the legislative branch of county government, the Council sets policies, enacts laws, and adopts budgets that guide an array of services for county residents.
The Council's nine councilmembers are elected on a non-partisan basis and serve four-year terms.
Each councilmember represents a geographical district of over 260,000 residents.
ask: What would they fund first, or cut, in the county budget?
Which county services would they change, and how?

entries.title: King County Director of Elections
entries.plain: Leads King County Elections, which serves a third of Washington's voters by mail: getting voters registered and their ballots cast and counted.

source.name: King County Elections, About us

quotes: Home to one-third of Washington State's voters, King County was the largest vote-by-mail jurisdiction in the world for many years prior to more widespread adoption in 2020.
the team at KCE is committed to ensuring all King County voters can get registered, cast their ballot, and make their voices heard.
ask: How would they keep elections accurate and secure?
How would they make voting easier for everyone?

entries.title: King County Assessor
entries.plain: Runs the office that values property in King County for property taxes, hears appeals of those values, and runs the property tax relief programs.

source.name: King County Assessor

quotes: we hope this site will help you with issues regarding property values, and the tax relief programs we administer.
You can also find information on your property's value, details and data on our property tax system, how to appeal your property value, and information on our office.
ask: How would they keep property values accurate and fair?
How would they make appeals and tax relief easier to use?

entries.title: Seattle Municipal Court judge
entries.plain: One of seven elected judges on Seattle's city court, the busiest of its kind in the state. It hears misdemeanor crimes (such as DUI, domestic violence, theft and trespass) and civil infractions.

source.name: Seattle Municipal Court, About us

quotes: Seattle Municipal Court is the largest limited jurisdiction court by case volume in Washington State with seven elected judges and five appointed magistrates .

Seattle Municipal Court handles all misdemeanor and gross misdemeanor crimes, civil infractions, and other offenses authorized under the Seattle Municipal Code and certain Revised Code of Washington Statutes.
Gross Misdemeanors: Crimes that carry a maximum sentence of 364 days in jail and a $5,000 fine, including offenses such as driving under the influence (DUI), domestic violence, theft, and trespass.

entries.title: King County District Court judge
entries.plain: A judge on the county's District Court, which hears misdemeanor crimes (such as DUI, reckless driving and fourth-degree assault) and smaller civil cases.

source.name: Washington Courts, A Guide to Washington State Courts (2011)

quotes: District courts are county courts and serve defined territories, both incorporated and unincorporated, within the counties.
District courts have jurisdiction over both criminal and civil cases. Criminal jurisdiction includes misdemeanors and gross misdemeanors cases that involve traffic or non-traffic offenses.
Examples include: Driving while under the influence of intoxicating liquor or drugs (DUI), reckless driving, driving with a suspended driver's license and assault in the fourth degree.

entries.title: Washington Supreme Court justice
entries.plain: One of nine justices on Washington's highest court. Its decisions become state law that every other court follows, and it sets the rules for all of the state's courts.

source.name: Washington Courts, A Guide to Washington State Courts (2011)

quotes: The Supreme Court is the state's highest court. Its opinions are published, become the law of the state, and set precedent for subsequent cases decided in Washington.
All nine justices hear and dispose of cases argued on the appeal calendar.
The Supreme Court is the final rule-making authority for all of the state's courts.

entries.title: Washington Court of Appeals judge
entries.plain: A judge on the court that hears most appeals from the county superior courts. It must take every appeal filed, and can uphold, overturn, change or send back a lower court's decision.

source.name: Washington Courts, A Guide to Washington State Courts (2011)

quotes: Most cases appealed from superior courts go directly to the Court of Appeals. It is a non-discretionary appellate court--it must accept all appeals filed with it. The Court of Appeals has authority to reverse (overrule), remand (send back to the lower court), modify, or affirm the decision of the lower court.

entries.title: Washington State Senator or Representative
entries.plain: Each legislative district elects one state senator (four-year term) and two state representatives (two-year terms). They vote on the bills that become state law, and on the state budget.

source.name: Washington State Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs, About the Legislature

quotes: Each district is served by one Senator and two House members.
Members of the Senate are elected to four-year terms, and House members are elected to two-year terms.
If a bill passes all of these steps, it then moves to the opposite chamber .
In odd-numbered years-the budget year-the Legislature meets for 105 days.
ask: Which state laws would they work to pass or change?
What would they put first in the state budget?

entries.title: Attorney General
entries.plain: Colorado's top lawyer, elected statewide. Runs the Department of Law, which upholds the U.S. and Colorado constitutions, defends state laws and officials when they're challenged in court, and works with law enforcement.

source.name: Colorado Attorney General, About us

quotes: The Colorado Attorney General is one of four independently elected statewide offices in Colorado and was established by the State Constitution upon statehood in 1876.
Upholding the United States and Colorado Constitutions.
Defending the laws and officers of the State of Colorado from legal challenge.
Advocating for policies that help law enforcement improve community safety.
ask: Which kinds of cases would they make a priority?
When would they take someone to court on the state's behalf?

entries.title: Secretary of State
entries.plain: Oversees Colorado's elections (the statewide voter list, checking petition signatures for ballot measures, campaign finance rules) and registers businesses and other public records.

source.name: Colorado Secretary of State, About the office

quotes: These varied duties are divided primarily between the Business & Licensing and Elections Divisions.
The basic mission of the Department of State is to collect, secure, and make accessible a wide variety of public records, ensure the integrity of elections, and enhance commerce.
Supervises elections, maintains statewide voter registration file, verifies initiative petition signatures, and administers the Campaign Finance Laws
ask: How would they run elections that are both secure and easy to vote in?
How would they make campaign money easier to follow?

entries.title: Larimer County Commissioner
entries.plain: One of three commissioners who make policy for Larimer County. Each is elected countywide, from one of three districts, for a four-year term.

source.name: Larimer County Board of County Commissioners

quotes: Larimer's three-member Board of County Commissioners is the main policy-making body in the County and works to represent the interest of the citizens of Larimer County at local, state and national levels.
Commissioners are elected at large from one of three geographic districts for four-year staggered terms.
ask: What would they change about county services or the county budget?
Which county issues would they put first?

entries.title: Keeping a justice (retention)
entries.plain: Supreme Court and Court of Appeal justices aren't picked in a race. The governor appoints them, a state commission confirms them, and then voters answer Yes or No on keeping each one: at the next governor's election, and again whenever they want another term.

source.name: LAist, 2026 voter guide to Court of Appeal justices

quotes: In California, appellate court justices are first appointed by the governor and then subject to approval by the Commission on Judicial Appointments. Newly confirmed justices have to face voters at the next gubernatorial election and when they want another term.

facts.plain: Since retention votes began in 1934, justices have kept their seats in 794 of 797 votes. No Court of Appeal justice has ever lost one; the three who lost were all on the Supreme Court, in 1986.

source.name: California Assembly Elections Committee, analysis of ACA 8 (2025)

quotes: Since the state's retention election process was created in 1934, no Court of Appeals justice has ever been defeated in a retention election, while three Supreme Court justices were defeated (all in 1986). In all, justices were retained in 794 of the 797 retention elections held in the state's history (99.6%).

facts.plain: Many voters leave these blank: regularly more than 25% of ballots, and over 40% in some recent elections, compared with 2% to 6% for statewide offices.

source.name: California Assembly Elections Committee, analysis of ACA 8 (2025)

quotes: The percentage of ballots that are left blank (commonly referred to as "drop-off") in retention elections regularly exceeds 25%, and has been more than 40% in some recent retention elections. By contrast, drop-off in elections for statewide office during the same time period typically has ranged from 2%-6%

facts.plain: LAist: “your vote here is largely about sending a signal on whether you support what they've done.”

source.name: LAist, 2026 voter guide to Court of Appeal justices

quotes: It's rare for a justice to lose a seat, so your vote here is largely about sending a signal on whether you support what they've done.

facts.plain: Leaving a question blank doesn’t affect the rest of your ballot: everything you do vote on still counts.

source.name: LAist, on undervoting

quotes: even if you've undervoted, the things you do vote on still count.

links.label: Read their recent opinions (the courts’ own lists)

entries.title: State Assembly member
entries.plain: A member of the Assembly, one of the two houses of California's Legislature. Members write bills, often from ideas people bring them, and vote on bills and on the state budget; with the Senate they can override a governor's veto by a two-thirds vote. Assembly terms are two years.

source.name: California State Senate, Citizens' Guide: Legislative Process

quotes: These ideas can come from anybody and the process begins when either an individual or group persuades a Member of the Legislature to author a bill.
If the Governor vetoes the bill, a two-thirds vote in each house is needed to override the veto.

facts.plain: The Legislature must pass the state budget by June 15 each year; the budget decides which services the state provides and who pays for them.

source.name: California State Senate, The Budget Process: A Citizen's Guide to Participation

quotes: After its introduction, the Legislature has until June 15 to pass the budget.
The final state budget determines which services are provided and who pays for them.

facts.plain: Assembly members serve two-year terms and senators four-year terms. As of 2015 each Assembly member represented about 475,000 people and each senator about 950,000.

source.name: California State Assembly, California's State Assembly (2015)

quotes: Members of the Assembly are elected for two-year terms, while Senators are elected for four-year terms, with one-half of the membership elected every two years.
Out of 38+ million Californians, each Member of the Assembly represents approximately 475,000 people, and each Senator represents approximately 950,000 people.

facts.plain: Nobody may serve more than 12 years in the Legislature in their lifetime, in the Senate, the Assembly or both.

source.name: California State Senate, FAQs

quotes: During his or her lifetime a person may serve no more than 12 years in the Senate, Assembly, or both, in any combination of terms.

ask: What would they put first in the state budget?
Which bills would they write first, and which would they vote against?
How would they hear from people in their district?

entries.title: State Senator
entries.plain: One of 40 members of the State Senate, the other house of California's Legislature, elected for four-year terms. Senators write bills, often from ideas people bring them, and vote on bills and on the state budget; with the Assembly they can override a governor's veto by a two-thirds vote.

source.name: California State Senate, Citizens' Guide: Legislative Process

quotes: These ideas can come from anybody and the process begins when either an individual or group persuades a Member of the Legislature to author a bill.
If the Governor vetoes the bill, a two-thirds vote in each house is needed to override the veto.

facts.plain: The Senate has 40 members with four-year terms; half begin every two years.

source.name: California State Senate, FAQs

quotes: The Senate has a membership of 40 Senators elected for 4-year terms, 20 to begin every 2 years.

facts.plain: The Legislature must pass the state budget by June 15 each year; the budget decides which services the state provides and who pays for them.

source.name: California State Senate, The Budget Process: A Citizen's Guide to Participation

quotes: After its introduction, the Legislature has until June 15 to pass the budget.
The final state budget determines which services are provided and who pays for them.

facts.plain: Assembly members serve two-year terms and senators four-year terms. As of 2015 each Assembly member represented about 475,000 people and each senator about 950,000.

source.name: California State Assembly, California's State Assembly (2015)

quotes: Members of the Assembly are elected for two-year terms, while Senators are elected for four-year terms, with one-half of the membership elected every two years.
Out of 38+ million Californians, each Member of the Assembly represents approximately 475,000 people, and each Senator represents approximately 950,000 people.

facts.plain: Nobody may serve more than 12 years in the Legislature in their lifetime, in the Senate, the Assembly or both.

source.name: California State Senate, FAQs

quotes: During his or her lifetime a person may serve no more than 12 years in the Senate, Assembly, or both, in any combination of terms.

ask: What would they put first in the state budget?
Which bills would they write first, and which would they vote against?
How would they hear from people in their district?

entries.title: Los Angeles County Sheriff
entries.plain: Runs the Sheriff's Department, the county's chief law enforcement agency. It polices most of the county's unincorporated areas and 42 cities that contract with it, guards courtrooms, and runs the county jails, which hold about 13,000 people in seven facilities.

source.name: Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors, Sheriff's Department budget summary (2025)

quotes: The Sheriff serves as the chief law enforcement officer of Los Angeles County, enforcing state laws and county ordinances across 77% of the county's unincorporated areas and all cities within the county.
The office provides law enforcement and traffic services to 42 cities, as well as agencies like the Los Angeles Superior Court and Metrolink.
Additionally, the Sheriff manages the care, placement, and secure housing of approximately 13,000 individuals in County jails across seven facilities.
Courtroom Security Services: Serving as bailiff and protecting judges and juries.
ask: What would they change about how deputies patrol and respond to calls?
How would they run the county jails?
How would they handle complaints about deputies?

entries.title: Los Angeles Community College District trustee
entries.plain: One of seven trustees who govern the Los Angeles Community College District. Trustees are elected by voters across the whole district (not one area) for four-year terms; three or four seats are up every two years.

source.name: Los Angeles Community College District, BuildLACCD: Leadership

quotes: The Los Angeles Community College District is governed by a seven-member Board.
Board members are elected at large for terms of four years.
Elections are held every two years, with three members being chosen at one election and four members at the other.

facts.plain: The district runs nine colleges. Voter-approved bonds (Propositions A and AA, Measure J) pay for building at them, reviewed by a citizens' oversight committee.

source.name: LACCD Citizens' Oversight Committee, Annual Report 2011-12

quotes: Over the past 83 years, the nine colleges combined have served more than three million students.

In it is a breakdown of the costs and a review of the progress made on the construction, renovation, up- grades, furnishings and equipment for projects at the nine colleges and the satellite campuses funded by Proposi- tion A, AA and Measure J.

ask: What would they put first in the district budget?
How would they help more students finish a degree, a certificate or a transfer?
How would they oversee spending from the construction bonds?

entries.title: Monterey Park City Council member
entries.plain: The City Council adopts Monterey Park's budget each year, which sets how much service residents get and what the city collects. It approves city contracts and spending, and adopts the city's service goals, policies and regulations.

source.name: City of Monterey Park, City Council

quotes: The City Council determines service levels and revenue obligations through the adoption of an annual budget, authorizes City contracts and expenditures, establishes municipal service goals and operating policies, and adopts regulatory measures necessary to establish community protection.
ask: What would they put first in the city budget?
Which city services would they add, keep or cut?
How would they keep residents informed and involved in decisions?

entries.title: Monterey Park City Treasurer
entries.plain: An elected official who oversees the safekeeping of the city's money and pays it out when the City Council orders it.

source.name: City of Monterey Park, Elected Officials

quotes: The City Treasurer is an elected position and is responsible to the electorate for overseeing the custody of the City monies and their disbursement upon order of the City Council.
ask: How would they keep the city's money safe?
How would they report to residents on the city's money?

entries.title: Montebello City Council member
entries.plain: One of five council members who set Montebello's overall policies and direction; a city manager runs day-to-day operations. Members serve four-year terms, pick one of themselves as mayor each year, and appoint residents to city commissions.

source.name: City of Montebello, Elected Officials

quotes: As a general-law city, Montebello operates through the Council - City Manager form of municipal government.
The five City Council members are elected to overlapping terms of four years and annually select one of their members to serve as Mayor.
The City Council is the legislative body responsible for the overall policies and direction for the City of Montebello.
The City Council appoints residents to serve on several commissions.
ask: What would they put first in the city budget?
Which city services would they add, keep or cut?
How would they keep residents informed and involved in decisions?

entries.title: Montebello Unified School District board member
entries.plain: A member of the board that governs Montebello Unified. The board sets the district's long-term direction, answers to the community for its schools' education and finances, and alone hires the superintendent who runs the district.

source.name: California State Auditor, Report 2017-104 on Montebello Unified (2017), Introduction

quotes: The board's primary role is to establish Montebello's long-term vision, maintain a basic organizational structure, and ensure educational and fiscal accountability to the community while providing community leadership.
The board is also solely responsible for employing the superintendent, who is the general administrator of all of Montebello's instructional and business operations.
ask: What would they put first in the district budget?
How would they judge whether the superintendent is doing a good job?
How would they report the district's finances to families?

entries.title: U.S. Senator
entries.plain: One of a state's two U.S. senators. The Senate and the House are the two chambers of Congress, the federal government's legislative branch. Only the Senate approves or rejects the president's nominees for federal judges and other top posts, approves treaties (by a two-thirds vote) and holds impeachment trials.

source.name: U.S. Senate, Powers and Procedures

quotes: The Senate has always jealously guarded its power to review and approve or reject presidential appointees to executive and judicial branch posts.
The Constitution gives the Senate the power to approve, by a two-thirds vote, treaties made by the executive branch.
The Senate has the sole power to conduct impeachment trials, essentially serving as jury and judge.

facts.plain: Congress has two chambers, the House and the Senate, and is the federal government's legislative branch.

source.name: U.S. House of Representatives, The House Explained

quotes: The House is one of Congress's two chambers (the other is the U.S. Senate), and part of the federal government's legislative branch.

facts.plain: Each state has two senators, who serve six-year terms. (The Constitution as written had state legislatures choose them.)

source.name: U.S. Senate, The Senate and the United States Constitution

quotes: The Senate of the United States shall be composed of two Senators from each State, chosen by the Legislature thereof, for six Years.

ask: Which federal laws would they work to pass or change first?
How would they decide whether to confirm a president's nominees?

entries.title: Governor (and Lieutenant Governor)
entries.plain: The governor decides what happens to every bill the Legislature passes: sign it, let it become law unsigned, or veto it. When a judge's seat opens, the governor picks the new judge from two or three nominees chosen by a nominating commission.

source.name: Colorado General Assembly, The Legislature at a Glance

quotes: If a bill passes, or is approved, by both the House and the Senate, it will go to the Governor.
The Governor can do three things with the bill: sign it into law, allow it to become law without his or her signature, or veto the billl.

facts.plain: The governor appoints Colorado's state judges from a short list of nominees.

source.name: Colorado Office of Judicial Performance Evaluation, Frequently Asked Questions

quotes: Each time a vacancy occurs, the Governor selects a new judge from a list of two or three highly qualified nominees chosen by a judicial nominating commission.

ask: Which kinds of bills would they sign, and which would they veto?
How would they choose judges from the nominees they are given?

entries.title: State Treasurer
entries.plain: Heads the State Treasury, which holds the state's money: it accounts for tax dollars from when they come in until they are paid out, invests them in the meantime in investments state law allows, and keeps enough cash on hand for daily needs. It also runs the state's unclaimed property program.

source.name: Colorado Department of the Treasury, Long Range Financial Plan (Nov. 2021)

quotes: The Colorado State Treasury is the constitutional custodian of the public's funds.
It is the Treasury's duty to manage and account for the citizen's tax dollars from the time they are received until the time they are disbursed.
As funds are deposited, they are invested in statutorily authorized investments.
Simultaneously, the Treasury ensures that sufficient funds are maintained in cash accounts to meet the State's daily cash needs.

The Treasury Department is organized into five distinct divisions: Administration (encompassing Accounting, Cash Management and Banking, Investments, Debt Management), CLIMBER, Secure Savings, Unclaimed Property, and Special Purpose.
ask: How would they invest the state's money, and how much risk would they take?
How would they report to the public on the state's money?

entries.title: State Senator or Representative
entries.plain: One of Colorado's 100 legislators (35 senators, 65 representatives), who make the state's laws and represent the people of their district. Bills are heard in committees, where the public can speak for or against them. Senators can serve two four-year terms in a row and representatives four two-year terms, then must sit out a term before running again.

source.name: Colorado General Assembly, The Legislature at a Glance

quotes: There are 100 legislators (35 Senators and 65 Representatives).
Our legislators make laws to improve the lives of people living in our state.
Legislators represent the people living in their districts.
In committee, a small group of legislators hear from the public about why a bill should or should not be made into law.
Senators are term limited to 2 four-year terms and representatives to 4 two-year terms.
Term limits are consecutive and members can run again after sitting out the length of a term.
ask: Which bills would they write or support first?
How would they hear from people in their district?

entries.title: Larimer County Clerk and Recorder
entries.plain: Runs three county services: elections (voter rolls, ballots, polling sites and counting), recording (deeds, liens and other public records), and vehicle titles and registration.

source.name: Larimer County 2022 Budget, Introduction & Overview

quotes: The Office of the Clerk and Recorder is responsible for recording deeds, liens and other documents in the permanent public record, providing motor vehicle services such as titling and registration, and overseeing elections in the County, including providing polling equipment and tabulating results, monitoring polling sites, providing ballots, and maintaining voter registration rolls.
ask: How would they run elections and show voters they were counted correctly?
How would they improve vehicle and recording services?

entries.title: Larimer County Sheriff
entries.plain: Runs the Larimer County Sheriff's Office, on a budget of almost $70 million a year. By law the sheriff handles law enforcement, the county jail, the courts (officer of the court, security, moving prisoners), and serves as fire warden and leads search and rescue and hazardous-materials response.

source.name: Larimer County Sheriff's Office, About

quotes: An annual budget of almost 70 million dollars is used to operate the agency in order to fulfill the statutory duties of the Sheriff.
The statutory duties of the Sheriff are: Law Enforcement Keeper of the Jail Officer of the Court Court Security Transportation of Prisoners Fire Warden Search and Rescue Hazardous Materials
ask: How would they run the county jail?
What would they put first in patrols and investigations?

entries.title: Seattle City Council member
entries.plain: The City Council makes Seattle's laws (ordinances), sets city policy and approves the city's budget.

source.name: Seattle City Council

quotes: The Seattle City Council establishes City policy through enactment of ordinances (laws) and adoption of resolutions.
The City Council also approves and adopts the City's budget.
ask: What would they put first in the city budget?
Which city services would they add, keep or cut?
How would they keep residents informed and involved in decisions?

entries.title: Keeping a judge (retention)
entries.plain: Colorado's judges aren't picked in a race. When a seat opens, the governor appoints a judge from two or three nominees a commission picks. After two years the judge is on the ballot for a Yes or No vote on keeping them, and again at the end of every term: 8 years for the Court of Appeals, 10 for the Supreme Court.

source.name: Colorado Office of Judicial Performance Evaluation, Frequently Asked Questions

quotes: In 1966, Colorado voters passed a constitutional amendment that abolished partisan elections for state court judges and established a new merit selection system for the nomination, appointment, and retention of state court judges.
Each time a vacancy occurs, the Governor selects a new judge from a list of two or three highly qualified nominees chosen by a judicial nominating commission.
The judge serves a two-year provisional term before his or her name is on the ballot for retention.

Once retained, the judge serves a fixed term - four years for county court judges, six years for district court judges, eight years for court of appeals judges, and ten years for supreme court justices - before his or her name is on a retention ballot again.

facts.plain: Before each vote, a state commission evaluates every judge on the ballot so voters have something to go on (its finding shows under each question).

source.name: Colorado Office of Judicial Performance Evaluation, Frequently Asked Questions

quotes: Commissions on judicial performance provide voters with fair, responsible, and constructive evaluations of judges and justices seeking retention in general elections.

facts.plain: From 1990 to 2025 voters kept 1,898 of 1,914 judges (99.2%): 99.7% of those the commissions recommended keeping, and 63.6% of those they recommended not keeping.

source.name: Colorado Office of Judicial Performance Evaluation, Fact Sheet

quotes: Colorado voters elected to retain 1,898 of the 1,914 (99.2%) judicial officers standing for retention since 1990.

Colorado voters retained 99.7% of the judges receiving "Retain" recommendations, 63.6% of those receiving "Do Not Retain" recommendations, and retained all judicial officers where commissions offered no opinion.
